## Today the robot walks

No reinforcement learning. No training. No neural network.

Everything today comes from **one linear differential equation** and the inverse
kinematics you wrote in Week 3.

1. Why walking is hard: the body has no motor of its own.
2. Where the floor can push: CoM, CoP, ZMP, the support polygon.
3. The model: the linear inverted pendulum — derived, solved, read.
4. The one number that decides balance: the **capture point**.
5. A gait: footsteps, a swinging leg, double support, IK. Then it walks.

This is **Layer 4** — control and planning — doing the whole job on its own.

---

## Colour code for the week {.smaller}

The same colours mean the same things in every equation and every drawing:

| symbol | meaning | colour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ${\color{#3b7dd8}{x,\ \dot x,\ \ddot x}}$ | the **centre of mass** (CoM): position, velocity, acceleration (horizontal) | <span style="color:#3b7dd8">blue</span> |
| ${\color{#e8743b}{p}}$ | the **ZMP** — where the floor's push acts | <span style="color:#e8743b">orange</span> |
| ${\color{#2a9d5c}{f}}$ | a **force** from the floor | <span style="color:#2a9d5c">green</span> |
| ${\color{#c0392b}{\omega}}$ | how fast the robot falls: $\omega = \sqrt{g/z_c}$ | <span style="color:#c0392b">red</span> |
| ${\color{#8e44ad}{\xi}}$ | the **capture point** | <span style="color:#8e44ad">purple</span> |

$z_c$ is the height of the centre of mass, $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, $m$ the
robot's mass (33.3 kg for the G1).

---

## Why walking is hard: count the motors {.smaller}

```{python}
try:
    import soc4180
except ImportError:
    %pip install -q "soc4180 @ git+https://github.com/gnoejh/soc4180.git"
    import soc4180

import numpy as np
import mujoco
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

model = soc4180.load_g1()
mass = float(model.body_mass.sum())
print(f"degrees of freedom  nv = {model.nv}   (6 for the floating pelvis + 29 hinges)")
print(f"motors              nu = {model.nu}")
print(f"unactuated             = {model.nv - model.nu}   <- the whole body's position and orientation")
print(f"total mass             = {mass:.1f} kg")
```

The G1 has 35 ways to move and 29 motors. The 6 missing ones are exactly the
pelvis's free joint: **there is no motor between the robot and the world.**
A system with fewer inputs than degrees of freedom is **underactuated**.

Every motor pushes one link against another *inside* the robot. Internal
forces come in equal and opposite pairs, so they cannot move the robot as a
whole. The next slide says what can.

---

## Newton, for the whole robot {.smaller}

Add up $F = ma$ over every link. The internal (motor) forces cancel in pairs,
and what is left is one equation for the **centre of mass** ${\color{#3b7dd8}{\mathbf{c}}}$:

$$m\,{\color{#3b7dd8}{\ddot{\mathbf{c}}}} \;=\; {\color{#2a9d5c}{\mathbf{f}_{\text{floor}}}} \;+\; m\,\mathbf{g}$$

- ${\color{#3b7dd8}{\ddot{\mathbf{c}}}}$ — how the CoM accelerates
- ${\color{#2a9d5c}{\mathbf{f}_{\text{floor}}}}$ — the sum of every contact force under the feet
- $m\mathbf{g}$ — gravity, which we cannot change

**The only thing that can move the body horizontally is the floor.** And the
floor has rules: it can **push** (never pull), only **where a foot touches it**,
and only as hard as **friction** allows sideways.

So the robot cannot say "move my body 10 cm forward". It can only move its
legs so that the floor pushes the body where it wants. That is why walking is
**deliberately falling and catching yourself**:

1. lean so gravity starts to carry the body forward,
2. let the stance foot's floor force steer it,
3. put the next foot where it will catch the fall.

---

## The broom on your hand {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.5, 3.3))
titles = ["upright: floor force through the CoM\nno turning, no fall",
          "leaning: floor force behind the CoM\nthe body accelerates forward",
          "catch: a new foot ahead of the CoM\nthe floor pushes it back"]
for ax, (lean, foot, title) in zip(axes, ((0.0, 0.0, titles[0]), (0.15, 0.0, titles[1]), (0.15, 0.30, titles[2]))):
    ax.axhline(0, color="0.3", lw=2)
    ax.fill_between([-0.4, 0.7], -0.05, 0, color="0.9")
    cx, cz = lean, 0.6
    ax.plot([foot, cx], [0, cz], color="0.5", lw=2.5)
    ax.plot(cx, cz, "o", ms=16, color="#3b7dd8")
    ax.annotate("", xy=(cx, cz - 0.22), xytext=(cx, cz), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=2, color="0.3"))
    ax.text(cx + 0.03, cz - 0.16, "$mg$", fontsize=10)
    d = np.array([cx - foot, cz]); d = 0.28 * d / np.linalg.norm(d)
    ax.annotate("", xy=(foot + d[0], d[1]), xytext=(foot, 0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=2.5, color="#2a9d5c"))
    ax.plot(foot, 0, "v", color="#e8743b", ms=10)
    if lean:
        ax.annotate("", xy=(cx + 0.14 * (1 if foot < cx else -1), cz + 0.08), xytext=(cx, cz + 0.08),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=2, color="#3b7dd8"))
    ax.set_xlim(-0.35, 0.65); ax.set_ylim(-0.08, 0.8); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9)
fig.text(0.5, 0.02, "green: the floor's push (along the leg);  orange: where it acts;  blue arrow: where the CoM accelerates",
         ha="center", fontsize=8.5, color="0.35")
fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.05, 1, 1)); plt.show()
```

Balancing a broom: you cannot push the top, only move the bottom. When the
floor's force points *through* the CoM nothing turns; when it points behind,
the body is flung forward — faster the further it leans. Walking uses that
fall on purpose, and ends it by putting a foot down ahead of the body.

---

## Two ways to walk {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
fig, (a0, a1) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 3.2))
for ax, title in ((a0, "static: the CoM (blue) never leaves the foot under it"),
                  (a1, "dynamic: the CoM travels between the feet")):
    for k in range(4):
        y = 0.12 if k % 2 == 0 else -0.12
        ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((0.2 * k - 0.085, y - 0.03), 0.17, 0.06, color="#e8743b", alpha=0.25))
    ax.set_xlim(-0.15, 0.8); ax.set_ylim(-0.2, 0.2); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xlabel("x forward (m)"); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
xs, ys = [], []
for k in range(4):                        # static: shift fully over each foot, then move
    y = 0.12 if k % 2 == 0 else -0.12
    xs += [0.2 * k - 0.05, 0.2 * k + 0.05]; ys += [y * 0.9, y * 0.9]
a0.plot(xs, ys, "-o", color="#3b7dd8", ms=3)
t = np.linspace(0, 0.6, 200)
a1.plot(t + 0.0, 0.059 * np.sin(np.pi * t / 0.2 + np.pi / 2), color="#3b7dd8", lw=2)
a0.set_ylabel("y left (m)")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Static walking** (left) carries the CoM all the way over each foot before
lifting the other: freeze it at any instant and it stays up. Slow — the look
of a 1985 robot. **Dynamic walking** (right) lets the CoM sway only about 6
centimetres and spend most of its time *between* the feet, over no foot at
all, falling toward the next one. Fast and efficient — and frozen mid-step it
falls. Both paths are sketches; the dynamic one's real shape is derived later
today from the LIPM.

Real humanoids combine the two ideas: a **plan** (where the feet and the body
should go) and **feedback** that uses the natural fall. Today is the plan.

---

## Where the floor pushes: CoP {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
xs_c = np.array([-0.05, 0.0, 0.05, 0.12])            # contact points along the foot
fz = np.array([60.0, 110.0, 90.0, 67.0])             # an illustrative split of 327 N
cop = (fz * xs_c).sum() / fz.sum()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.0))
for ax, title in zip(axes, ("what the floor does: many pushes", "what it is equivalent to: one push at the CoP")):
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((-0.06, 0.0), 0.19, 0.035, color="0.75"))
    ax.axhline(0, color="0.3", lw=2)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.1, 0.2); ax.set_ylim(-0.4, 0.06); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9)
for x, f in zip(xs_c, fz):
    axes[0].annotate("", xy=(x, 0.0), xytext=(x, -f / 1000), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=2, color="#2a9d5c"))
    axes[0].text(x, -f / 1000 - 0.03, f"{f:.0f} N", ha="center", fontsize=8, color="#2a9d5c")
axes[1].annotate("", xy=(cop, 0.0), xytext=(cop, -fz.sum() / 1000), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=3, color="#e8743b"))
axes[1].text(cop + 0.01, -0.25, f"{fz.sum():.0f} N at x = {cop:+.3f} m", fontsize=8.5, color="#e8743b")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Many small upward forces ${\color{#2a9d5c}{f_i}} \ge 0$ at contact points $x_i$
act like **one** force of size $\sum_i f_i$ at the **centre of pressure**:

$${\color{#e8743b}{p}} = \frac{\sum_i {\color{#2a9d5c}{f_i}}\, x_i}{\sum_i {\color{#2a9d5c}{f_i}}}
 = \sum_i w_i\,x_i, \qquad w_i = \frac{{\color{#2a9d5c}{f_i}}}{\sum_j {\color{#2a9d5c}{f_j}}} \ge 0,\ \ \sum_i w_i = 1 .$$

The weights are **non-negative and sum to one** (the floor only pushes), so
${\color{#e8743b}{p}}$ is a weighted average of the contact points: it lies
between them, **inside the support polygon**, always. The forces above are
illustrative; the geometry is not.

---

## The ZMP, and the balance rule {.smaller}

The **Zero Moment Point** is the point on the floor about which gravity plus
the body's inertia produce **no tipping moment** (no moment about horizontal
axes). On flat ground it is the same point as the CoP — the two names come from
two ways of computing it, one from the motion, one from the forces.

The rule that follows from the last slide:

> **The ZMP must be inside the support polygon.** A motion that would need it
> outside cannot happen with the feet flat: the foot rolls about its edge
> instead, and no ankle torque can stop that.

- one foot on the floor: the polygon is that foot, about 17 × 6 cm on the G1
- both feet down: the convex hull around both feet (**double support**)
- walking: the polygon changes shape every step, and for most of each step it
  is one small foot

The whole gait is an argument about keeping the orange point in the shaded
area — which we measure at the end of the lecture.

---

## Our support polygon {.smaller}

Each G1 foot touches the floor through four small spheres. Their spread *is* the polygon:

```{python}
pts = [(model.geom_pos[g][0], model.geom_pos[g][1])
       for g in range(model.ngeom)
       if mujoco.mj_id2name(model, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_BODY, model.geom_bodyid[g])
       == "left_ankle_roll_link"
       and model.geom_type[g] == mujoco.mjtGeom.mjGEOM_SPHERE]
pts = np.array(pts)
print("contact points in the foot frame (x, y):")
print(pts)
print(f"\nfoot length {np.ptp(pts[:,0]):.3f} m, width {np.ptp(pts[:,1]):.3f} m")
```

A single foot gives you about 17 cm by 6 cm to balance a 33 kg robot on. That is
the entire margin.

---

## The polygon, drawn from the model {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
data = soc4180.keyframe_data(model, "stand")
mujoco.mj_forward(model, data)
feet_xy = {}
for side, col in (("left", "#3b7dd8"), ("right", "#e8743b")):
    body = mujoco.mj_name2id(model, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_BODY, f"{side}_ankle_roll_link")
    feet_xy[side] = np.array([data.geom_xpos[g][:2] for g in range(model.ngeom)
                              if model.geom_bodyid[g] == body
                              and model.geom_type[g] == mujoco.mjtGeom.mjGEOM_SPHERE])

def hull(points):
    """Convex hull, counter-clockwise (Andrew's monotone chain)."""
    pts = sorted(map(tuple, points))
    def half(seq):
        h = []
        for p in seq:
            while len(h) >= 2:
                (ax_, ay_), (bx_, by_) = np.subtract(h[-1], h[-2]), np.subtract(p, h[-2])
                if ax_ * by_ - ay_ * bx_ > 0:      # left turn: keep it
                    break
                h.pop()
            h.append(p)
        return h
    lower, upper = half(pts), half(pts[::-1])
    return np.array(lower[:-1] + upper[:-1])

com = data.subtree_com[0][:2]
both = hull(np.vstack(list(feet_xy.values())))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.6))
ax.fill(both[:, 0], both[:, 1], color="0.85", label="double support: both feet")
for side, col in (("left", "#3b7dd8"), ("right", "#e8743b")):
    h = hull(feet_xy[side])
    ax.fill(h[:, 0], h[:, 1], color=col, alpha=0.5, label=f"{side} foot alone")
    ax.plot(feet_xy[side][:, 0], feet_xy[side][:, 1], "o", color=col, ms=5)
ax.plot(com[0], com[1], "r*", ms=14, label="centre of mass, projected")
ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlabel("x forward (m)"); ax.set_ylabel("y left (m)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.14), ncol=2); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax.set_title("support polygons at `stand`: the ZMP may live only in the shaded areas", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"centre of mass projects to x = {com[0]:+.3f}, y = {com[1]:+.3f}")
```

Standing on both feet the polygon is the big grey shape. Lift one foot and it
collapses to a single patch — and while standing still, the CoM (red star)
has to be above it.

---

## The Linear Inverted Pendulum Model {.smaller}

Replace the 29-joint robot with the simplest thing that can fall over:

- all the mass in **one point** at the CoM, ${\color{#3b7dd8}{x}}$ horizontally
- a **massless leg** from that point to the floor, touching at ${\color{#e8743b}{p}}$
- one assumption that makes it solvable: **the CoM stays at constant height** $z_c$

The legs can hold the height constant (they are servo-controlled, and the IK
will be told to keep the pelvis level), so the model gives up only the
vertical motion. What is left is one equation:

$${\color{#3b7dd8}{\ddot{x}}} \;=\; {\color{#c0392b}{\omega^2}}\,({\color{#3b7dd8}{x}} - {\color{#e8743b}{p}}),
\qquad {\color{#c0392b}{\omega}} = \sqrt{g / z_c}$$

- ${\color{#3b7dd8}{x}} - {\color{#e8743b}{p}}$ — how far the CoM is from the point the floor pushes at
- ${\color{#c0392b}{\omega^2}}$ — how strongly that distance turns into acceleration

Read it in words: **the CoM accelerates away from the ZMP, harder the further away it is.**
That is a hill, not a valley. The next two slides derive it; the two after
that solve it.

---

## Where the equation comes from: the forces {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
zc, xm, pz = 0.60, 0.14, 0.0
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.0))
ax.axhline(0, color="0.3", lw=2); ax.fill_between([-0.3, 0.5], -0.06, 0, color="0.9")
ax.plot([pz, xm], [0, zc], color="0.5", lw=2, ls="--")                       # massless leg
ax.plot(xm, zc, "o", ms=18, color="#3b7dd8"); ax.text(xm + 0.03, zc, "$m$", fontsize=12, va="center")
ax.plot(pz, 0, "v", color="#e8743b", ms=10); ax.text(pz, -0.045, "ZMP  $p$", ha="center", fontsize=10, color="#e8743b")
ax.annotate("", xy=(xm, zc - 0.22), xytext=(xm, zc), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=2, color="0.3"))
ax.text(xm + 0.02, zc - 0.13, "$mg$", color="0.3", fontsize=11)
F = np.array([xm - pz, zc]); F = 0.33 * F / np.linalg.norm(F)
ax.annotate("", xy=(pz + F[0], F[1]), xytext=(pz, 0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=2.5, color="#2a9d5c"))
ax.text(pz + F[0] - 0.02, F[1] + 0.03, "$f$ (along the leg)", color="#2a9d5c", fontsize=10, ha="right")
ax.plot([xm, xm], [0, zc], ":", color="0.6")
ax.annotate("", xy=(xm, 0.30), xytext=(pz, 0.30), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", lw=1.2))
ax.text((pz + xm) / 2, 0.32, "$x - p$", ha="center", fontsize=11)
ax.annotate("", xy=(xm + 0.09, zc), xytext=(xm + 0.09, 0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", lw=1.2))
ax.text(xm + 0.11, zc / 2, "$z_c$ (held constant)", fontsize=10, va="center")
ax.set_xlim(-0.3, 0.55); ax.set_ylim(-0.08, 0.8); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

A **massless** leg cannot carry a moment, so the floor's force ${\color{#2a9d5c}{\mathbf{f}}}$
must point **along the leg**, from ${\color{#e8743b}{p}}$ to the mass. Its two
components are therefore in the ratio of the leg's two sides:

$$\frac{{\color{#2a9d5c}{f_x}}}{{\color{#2a9d5c}{f_z}}} = \frac{{\color{#3b7dd8}{x}} - {\color{#e8743b}{p}}}{z_c}.$$

---

## Where the equation comes from: three lines {.smaller}

**Step 1 — vertical.** The height is constant, so the vertical acceleration is
zero and Newton gives ${\color{#2a9d5c}{f_z}} - mg = m\,\ddot z = 0$:

$${\color{#2a9d5c}{f_z}} = mg .$$

**Step 2 — horizontal.** Newton again, with the ratio from the drawing:

$$m\,{\color{#3b7dd8}{\ddot{x}}} = {\color{#2a9d5c}{f_x}}
 = {\color{#2a9d5c}{f_z}}\,\frac{{\color{#3b7dd8}{x}} - {\color{#e8743b}{p}}}{z_c}
 = mg\,\frac{{\color{#3b7dd8}{x}} - {\color{#e8743b}{p}}}{z_c}.$$

**Step 3 — divide by $m$:**

$${\color{#3b7dd8}{\ddot{x}}} = \frac{g}{z_c}\,({\color{#3b7dd8}{x}} - {\color{#e8743b}{p}})
 = {\color{#c0392b}{\omega^2}}\,({\color{#3b7dd8}{x}} - {\color{#e8743b}{p}}).$$

**The same result, as a moment balance.** Multiply Step 2 by $z_c$:
$m z_c\,{\color{#3b7dd8}{\ddot x}} = mg\,({\color{#3b7dd8}{x}} - {\color{#e8743b}{p}})$.
The right side is gravity's moment about ${\color{#e8743b}{p}}$ (weight × lever arm);
the left side is the moment of the "inertial force" $m\ddot x$ at height $z_c$.
Setting them equal is exactly "zero moment about the ZMP" — which is where the
point gets its name. It is an **equation of motion obtained from a moment
balance**, not itself a torque.

Units check: $g/z_c$ is $\mathrm{(m/s^2)/m} = \mathrm{1/s^2}$, so ${\color{#c0392b}{\omega}}$ is in $1/\mathrm{s}$.

---

## Solving it exactly {.smaller}

Hold ${\color{#e8743b}{p}}$ fixed (one foot planted) and write $u = {\color{#3b7dd8}{x}} - {\color{#e8743b}{p}}$.
Then $\ddot u = {\color{#c0392b}{\omega^2}} u$ — a linear ODE with constant coefficients.

**Step 1 — try $u = e^{rt}$:** $r^2 e^{rt} = {\color{#c0392b}{\omega^2}} e^{rt}$, so $r = \pm{\color{#c0392b}{\omega}}$ and

$$u(t) = A\,e^{{\color{#c0392b}{\omega}} t} + B\,e^{-{\color{#c0392b}{\omega}} t}.$$

**Step 2 — a second-order equation needs two starting facts.** Where the CoM is
and how fast it is going at $t = 0$:

$${\color{#3b7dd8}{x}}(0) = x_0, \qquad {\color{#3b7dd8}{\dot x}}(0) = v_0 .$$

$v_0$ is not a new variable of the model: it is the **initial velocity**, the
second integration constant. Plugging in: $A + B = x_0 - {\color{#e8743b}{p}}$ and
${\color{#c0392b}{\omega}}(A - B) = v_0$.

**Step 3 — solve for $A, B$ and use $\cosh = (e^{+} + e^{-})/2$, $\sinh = (e^{+} - e^{-})/2$:**

$${\color{#3b7dd8}{x}}(t) = {\color{#e8743b}{p}} + (x_0 - {\color{#e8743b}{p}})\cosh({\color{#c0392b}{\omega}} t) + \frac{v_0}{{\color{#c0392b}{\omega}}}\sinh({\color{#c0392b}{\omega}} t),
\qquad
{\color{#3b7dd8}{\dot x}}(t) = (x_0 - {\color{#e8743b}{p}})\,{\color{#c0392b}{\omega}}\sinh({\color{#c0392b}{\omega}} t) + v_0\cosh({\color{#c0392b}{\omega}} t).$$

Released at rest ($v_0 = 0$) it is just ${\color{#e8743b}{p}} + (x_0 - {\color{#e8743b}{p}})\cosh({\color{#c0392b}{\omega}} t)$:
starts gently, then runs away. No numerical integration anywhere — this is
the formula the controller evaluates, 500 times a second.

---

## Reading the numbers {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
lipm = soc4180.LIPM(com_height=0.60)
print(f"omega = sqrt(9.81/0.60) = {lipm.omega:.3f} 1/s      1/omega = {1/lipm.omega:.3f} s  <- the time constant")
for t in (0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4):
    x, v = lipm.evolve(x0=0.0, v0=0.0, zmp=0.05, t=t)
    print(f"  t = {t:.1f} s   x = {x:+.4f} m   v = {v:+.4f} m/s   distance from the ZMP x{np.cosh(lipm.omega * t):5.2f}")

tt = np.linspace(0, 0.8, 200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 2.6))
ax.plot(tt, [0.05 - lipm.evolve(0.0, 0.0, 0.05, t)[0] for t in tt], color="#3b7dd8", lw=2, label="distance from the ZMP (m)")
for k in (1, 2, 3):
    ax.axvline(k / lipm.omega, color="#c0392b", ls=":", lw=1)
    ax.text(k / lipm.omega + 0.005, 0.02 + 0.08 * k, f"{k}/ω", color="#c0392b", fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlabel("time since release (s)"); ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The CoM starts **5 cm behind** the ZMP ($x_0 = 0$, ${\color{#e8743b}{p}} = 0.05$), at rest.
In 0.1 s it has moved 4 mm; in 0.2 s, 17 mm; in 0.4 s, 81 mm. The distance
grows like $\cosh({\color{#c0392b}{\omega}} t)$ — roughly **×e every
$1/{\color{#c0392b}{\omega}}$ = 0.25 s** once it gets going. A step of 0.65 s
is 2.6 time constants: whatever error the step starts with is multiplied by
about $\cosh 2.6 \approx 7$ by its end. That is the budget a walking
controller works within, and why a walker must act every step.

---

## Every possible motion, in one picture {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
w = lipm.omega
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.8))
U, V = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-0.1, 0.1, 17), np.linspace(-0.4, 0.4, 17))
ax.streamplot(U, V, V, w**2 * U, color="0.75", density=1.0, linewidth=0.8)   # (u, v)' = (v, w^2 u)
u = np.linspace(-0.1, 0.1, 2)
ax.plot(u, -w * u, color="#2a9d5c", lw=3, label=r"$\dot x = -\omega (x-p)$: comes to rest over the ZMP")
ax.plot(u, +w * u, color="#c0392b", lw=3, label=r"$\dot x = +\omega (x-p)$: runs away fastest")
ax.plot(0.05, 0, "o", color="#3b7dd8", ms=8); ax.text(0.052, 0.02, "released 5 cm\nfrom the ZMP", fontsize=8, color="#3b7dd8")
ax.set_xlim(-0.1, 0.1); ax.set_ylim(-0.4, 0.4)
ax.set_xlabel(r"distance from the ZMP  $x - p$ (m)"); ax.set_ylabel(r"velocity $\dot x$ (m/s)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right"); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Each grey curve is one possible motion, in the plane of **(distance from the
ZMP, velocity)**. Two straight lines are special. On the <span style="color:#2a9d5c">green</span>
one the CoM moves *toward* the ZMP at exactly the speed that brings it to rest
on top of it — only $e^{-\omega t}$ is present. On the <span style="color:#c0392b">red</span>
one only $e^{+\omega t}$ is present. Every other motion is a mix, and the
$e^{+\omega t}$ part eventually wins: **the robot falls to the side of the green line it is on.**

---

## The capture point {.smaller}

How far is the state from the green line? Measure it with one number:

$${\color{#8e44ad}{\xi}} \;=\; {\color{#3b7dd8}{x}} + \frac{{\color{#3b7dd8}{\dot x}}}{{\color{#c0392b}{\omega}}}$$

**Step 1 — differentiate:** ${\color{#8e44ad}{\dot\xi}} = {\color{#3b7dd8}{\dot x}} + {\color{#3b7dd8}{\ddot x}}/{\color{#c0392b}{\omega}}$.

**Step 2 — use the LIPM**, ${\color{#3b7dd8}{\ddot x}} = {\color{#c0392b}{\omega^2}}({\color{#3b7dd8}{x}} - {\color{#e8743b}{p}})$:
${\color{#8e44ad}{\dot\xi}} = {\color{#3b7dd8}{\dot x}} + {\color{#c0392b}{\omega}}({\color{#3b7dd8}{x}} - {\color{#e8743b}{p}}) = {\color{#c0392b}{\omega}}\big({\color{#3b7dd8}{x}} + {\color{#3b7dd8}{\dot x}}/{\color{#c0392b}{\omega}} - {\color{#e8743b}{p}}\big)$.

$${\color{#8e44ad}{\dot\xi}} = {\color{#c0392b}{\omega}}\,({\color{#8e44ad}{\xi}} - {\color{#e8743b}{p}})
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
{\color{#8e44ad}{\xi}}(t) - {\color{#e8743b}{p}} = \big({\color{#8e44ad}{\xi_0}} - {\color{#e8743b}{p}}\big)\,e^{{\color{#c0392b}{\omega}} t}$$

A second-order equation became a **first-order** one, and all of the danger
is in it: ${\color{#8e44ad}{\xi}}$ runs away from ${\color{#e8743b}{p}}$ exponentially, and nothing else does.
(The other combination, $\eta = x - \dot x/\omega$, obeys $\dot\eta = -\omega(\eta - p)$
and settles by itself — exercise 2.) ${\color{#8e44ad}{\xi}} = {\color{#e8743b}{p}}$ is exactly the green line of the last slide.

**Its meaning.** Put the foot — the ZMP — **on** ${\color{#8e44ad}{\xi}}$. Then
${\color{#8e44ad}{\dot\xi}} = 0$, ${\color{#8e44ad}{\xi}}$ stays put, and the CoM
slides onto it and stops. **The capture point is where you must step to come
to rest in one step.** Step short of it and you keep falling forward; step
beyond it and you are pushed back.

---

## Capture, drawn {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
x0, v0 = 0.0, 0.30                                   # the CoM over the foot, moving 0.3 m/s
xi = x0 + v0 / w
tt = np.linspace(0, 1.2, 200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 3.2))
for p, col, lab in ((xi - 0.03, "#c0392b", "step 3 cm short: keeps falling forward"),
                    (xi, "#8e44ad", "step on the capture point: comes to rest"),
                    (xi + 0.03, "#2a9d5c", "step 3 cm beyond: pushed back")):
    ax.plot(tt, [lipm.evolve(x0, v0, p, t)[0] for t in tt], color=col, lw=2, label=lab)
    ax.axhline(p, color=col, ls=":", lw=1)
ax.set_ylim(-0.02, 0.16); ax.set_xlabel("time after the step (s)"); ax.set_ylabel("CoM x (m)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left"); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"CoM at x = {x0} m moving {v0} m/s:  capture point = x + v/omega = {xi:.4f} m ahead")
```

A body moving at 0.3 m/s needs a foot **7.4 cm ahead** to stop in one step. A
G1 foot reaches 12 cm in front of the ankle, so in this model the ankle alone
could just about absorb it; twice the speed needs 15 cm and a step. Week 11's
planner found stepping by search; this is the reason it had to.

---

## The trick: choose the start so the end is right {.smaller}

A gait is not about predicting where the robot falls. It is about choosing
the motion so that at the end of the step (time $T$) the CoM is where the
next step needs it, ${\color{#3b7dd8}{x}}(T) = x_T$. That is a **boundary
value problem**: one condition at each end instead of two at the start.

**Solve for $v_0$** from the solution of three slides ago, setting $t = T$:

$$x_T = {\color{#e8743b}{p}} + (x_0 - {\color{#e8743b}{p}})\cosh({\color{#c0392b}{\omega}} T) + \frac{v_0}{{\color{#c0392b}{\omega}}}\sinh({\color{#c0392b}{\omega}} T)
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
v_0 = {\color{#c0392b}{\omega}}\,\frac{x_T - {\color{#e8743b}{p}} - (x_0 - {\color{#e8743b}{p}})\cosh({\color{#c0392b}{\omega}} T)}{\sinh({\color{#c0392b}{\omega}} T)} .$$

It is linear in $v_0$, so there is exactly one answer. "Run it backwards"
means *reason from the end you want to the start you need* — not integrate
backwards in time. In capture-point terms it is the same idea: ${\color{#8e44ad}{\xi}}(T)$
is fixed by where you want to end, and ${\color{#8e44ad}{\xi_0}} = {\color{#e8743b}{p}} + ({\color{#8e44ad}{\xi_T}} - {\color{#e8743b}{p}})\,e^{-{\color{#c0392b}{\omega}} T}$
— the exponential that explodes forward shrinks when you go from the goal back to now.

```{python}
T = 0.65
v0 = lipm.bvp_velocity(x0=-0.07, xT=+0.07, zmp=0.0, T=T)
xT, vT = lipm.evolve(-0.07, v0, 0.0, T)
print(f"from x0 = -0.07 m to xT = +0.07 m over the stance foot at p = 0, in T = {T} s")
print(f"  required launch velocity v0 = {v0:+.4f} m/s  ->  arrives at {xT:+.4f} m with {vT:+.4f} m/s")
```

**Each step is one boundary value problem.** Chain them — every step starting
where the last ended — and you have a gait.

---

## The sideways problem {.smaller}

Sideways, each step's stance foot is at ${\color{#e8743b}{p}} = \pm w$ (the
G1 stands with $w = 0.119$ m). Ask for a **periodic** gait: each step the
mirror image of the last, $(y_T, v_T) = (-y_0, -v_0)$.

**Step 1 — the two ends**, from the solution with ${\color{#e8743b}{p}} = w$, $C = \cosh{\color{#c0392b}{\omega}}T$, $S = \sinh{\color{#c0392b}{\omega}}T$:

$$-y_0 = w + (y_0 - w)\,C + \frac{v_0}{\omega}S, \qquad -v_0 = (y_0 - w)\,\omega S + v_0\,C .$$

**Step 2 — the second equation gives $v_0$:** $v_0(1 + C) = (w - y_0)\,\omega S$, so
$v_0 = \omega\,(w - y_0)\,S/(1 + C)$.

**Step 3 — put it in the first.** Using $S^2 = C^2 - 1 = (C-1)(C+1)$, the $v_0$ term is
$(w - y_0)(C - 1)$, and the right side collapses:
$w + (y_0 - w)C + (w - y_0)(C - 1) = y_0$. So $-y_0 = y_0$:

$$y_0 = 0, \qquad v_0 = {\color{#c0392b}{\omega}}\,w\,\frac{\sinh({\color{#c0392b}{\omega}} T)}{1 + \cosh({\color{#c0392b}{\omega}} T)} = {\color{#c0392b}{\omega}}\,w\,\tanh\!\left(\tfrac{{\color{#c0392b}{\omega}} T}{2}\right).$$

**The CoM crosses the midline exactly at each support exchange**, moving toward
the new stance foot at $v_0$. It sways toward the foot, gravity (pulling it
*away* from the ZMP, i.e. back to the middle) turns it round, and it arrives at
the midline with the mirrored velocity.

```{python}
wy = 0.119
vy = lipm.lateral_periodic_velocity(zmp_y=wy, step_time=T)
sway = [lipm.evolve(0.0, vy, wy, f * T)[0] for f in np.linspace(0, 1, 41)]
print(f"v0 = omega w tanh(omega T / 2) = {lipm.omega * wy * np.tanh(lipm.omega * T / 2):+.4f} m/s   package: {vy:+.4f}")
print(f"maximum sway {max(sway):.4f} m (the foot is at {wy} m);   back on the midline at t = T: {sway[-1]:+.1e} m")
```

---

## Forward and sideways, drawn {.smaller}

```{python}

fig, (ax0, ax1) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 3.8))

tt = np.linspace(0, T, 60)
for v in (0.0, 0.2, 0.4):
    ax0.plot(tt, [lipm.evolve(-0.07, v, 0.0, t)[0] for t in tt], color="0.6", lw=1.2,
             label="wrong starts: $v_0$ = 0, 0.2, 0.4 m/s" if v == 0 else None)
v0 = lipm.bvp_velocity(-0.07, +0.07, 0.0, T)
ax0.plot(tt, [lipm.evolve(-0.07, v0, 0.0, t)[0] for t in tt], color="#3b7dd8", lw=2.5,
         label=f"boundary value solution, $v_0$ = {v0:.3f} m/s")
ax0.plot([0, T], [-0.07, 0.07], "ko"); ax0.axhline(0, color="#e8743b", lw=1, ls=":")
ax0.text(0.01, 0.005, "ZMP (the stance foot)", fontsize=8, color="#e8743b")
ax0.set_xlim(0, T); ax0.set_ylim(-0.12, 0.2)
ax0.set_xlabel("time in the step (s)"); ax0.set_ylabel("forward $x$ (m)")
ax0.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left"); ax0.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax0.set_title("forward: too slow it falls back, too fast it runs away", fontsize=10)

ys, ts, y, v = [], [], 0.0, vy
for k in range(4):
    zmp = wy if k % 2 == 0 else -wy
    for t in np.linspace(0, T, 40):
        ys.append(lipm.evolve(y, v, zmp, t)[0]); ts.append(k * T + t)
    y, v = lipm.evolve(y, v, zmp, T)
    ax1.hlines(zmp, k * T, (k + 1) * T, color="#e8743b", lw=6, alpha=0.4 if zmp > 0 else 0.7)
ax1.plot(ts, ys, color="#3b7dd8", lw=2, label="centre of mass $y$")
ax1.axhline(0, color="k", lw=0.8, ls=":")
ax1.set_xlabel("time (s)"); ax1.set_ylabel("lateral $y$ (m)"); ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax1.text(0.02, wy - 0.03, "ZMP on the left foot", fontsize=8, color="#e8743b")
ax1.text(T + 0.02, -wy + 0.015, "ZMP on the right foot", fontsize=8, color="#e8743b")
ax1.set_title("sideways: sway toward the stance foot, turn, cross the midline", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Left: the grey curves start with the wrong $v_0$ and miss; the one computed
from the boundary value problem lands exactly at $x_T$. Right: four steps of
the periodic sway — it never reaches the foot it leans toward (5.9 cm of a

## Planning the footsteps

```{python}
params = soc4180.GaitParams()
print(f"step length {params.step_length} m, step time {params.step_time} s, "
      f"clearance {params.step_height} m")
print(f"double support {params.double_support*100:.0f}% at each end of the step\n")

for k, (support, support_xy, swing_from, swing_to) in enumerate(
        soc4180.footstep_plan(params)[:5]):
    print(f"  step {k}: stand on {support:5s} at x={support_xy[0]:+.2f}  "
          f"swing {swing_from[0]:+.2f} -> {swing_to[0]:+.2f}")
```

The first step is a half stride, because both feet start level and a full stride
would over-reach. Each forward boundary value problem runs from half a stride
*behind* the stance foot to half a stride *ahead* of it — the CoM passes over
each foot at mid-step.

---

## Swinging the leg: the formulas {.smaller}

Let $s \in [0, 1]$ be the fraction of the step. The swing foot moves only in
the middle part; ${\color{#e8743b}{d}}$ = 0.20 is the double-support fraction at each end:

$$\sigma = \operatorname{clip}\!\left(\frac{s - {\color{#e8743b}{d}}}{1 - 2{\color{#e8743b}{d}}},\ 0,\ 1\right)
\qquad(\sigma = 0 \text{ until } s = d,\ \ \sigma = 1 \text{ after } s = 1 - d)$$

**Forward** — a cycloid-like blend from $x_A$ to $x_B$:

$$x_{\text{foot}} = x_A + (x_B - x_A)\left(\sigma - \frac{\sin 2\pi\sigma}{2\pi}\right),
\qquad \frac{d x_{\text{foot}}}{d\sigma} = (x_B - x_A)\,(1 - \cos 2\pi\sigma).$$

The velocity factor $1 - \cos 2\pi\sigma$ is **0 at $\sigma = 0$ and at
$\sigma = 1$** and largest (2) at mid-swing: the foot leaves gently and lands
at rest. A straight line, $x_A + (x_B - x_A)\sigma$, would jump from standing to
full speed — a jolt the servos cannot follow, and a foot still sliding when
it lands.

**Up** — lift and lower, peak $h$ = 10 cm at mid-swing, zero vertical speed at both ends:

$$z_{\text{foot}} = z_0 + h\,\frac{1 - \cos 2\pi\sigma}{2}.$$

The foot must clear the floor — dragged, it trips — and must arrive vertically
at rest, or the landing is an impact.

---

## The plan and the swing, drawn {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
from soc4180.walking import _swing_xy, _swing_z

fig, (ax0, ax1) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 3.6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.6, 1]})
plan = soc4180.footstep_plan(params)
for k, (support, support_xy, swing_from, swing_to) in enumerate(plan):
    swing = "left" if support == "right" else "right"
    col = "#3b7dd8" if swing == "left" else "#e8743b"
    ax0.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((swing_to[0] - 0.085, swing_to[1] - 0.03), 0.17, 0.06,
                                color=col, alpha=0.35))
    ax0.text(swing_to[0], swing_to[1], str(k), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8)
    ax0.annotate("", xy=swing_to, xytext=swing_from,
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=col, lw=1, alpha=0.8))
for side, y0 in (("left", +params.stance_width), ("right", -params.stance_width)):
    ax0.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((-0.085, y0 - 0.03), 0.17, 0.06, fill=False, ls="--", color="0.5"))
ax0.set_xlim(-0.15, 1.0); ax0.set_ylim(-0.25, 0.25); ax0.set_aspect("equal")
ax0.set_xlabel("x forward (m)"); ax0.set_ylabel("y left (m)")

s = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
ds = params.double_support
s_sw = np.clip((s - ds) / (1 - 2 * ds), 0, 1)
ax1.plot(s, [_swing_xy(0.0, params.step_length, v) for v in s_sw], lw=2, label="forward $x$ (m)")
ax1.plot(s, [_swing_z(params.step_height, params.foot_height, v) for v in s_sw], lw=2, label="height $z$ (m)")
ax1.axvspan(0, ds, color="0.85"); ax1.axvspan(1 - ds, 1, color="0.85")
ax1.text(ds / 2, 0.105, "double\nsupport", ha="center", fontsize=8, color="0.4")

ax1.set_title("the swing: at rest at both ends", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**The plan** says *where* each foot lands (left); **the swing** says *how* it
gets there (right). Walking needs both: a plan without a swing teleports the
feet, a swing without a plan moves them nicely to the wrong place.

---

## Double support: why the weight needs both feet {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 2.4))
phases = [(0, ds, "both\nfeet", "0.8"), (ds, 1 - ds, "right foot only (left swings)", "#e8743b"),
          (1 - ds, 1 + ds, "both\nfeet", "0.8"), (1 + ds, 2 - ds, "left foot only (right swings)", "#3b7dd8"),
          (2 - ds, 2, "both\nfeet", "0.8")]
for a, b, lab, col in phases:
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((a * T, 0), (b - a) * T, 1, color=col, alpha=0.35))
    ax.text((a + b) / 2 * T, 0.5, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlim(0, 2 * T); ax.set_ylim(0, 1); ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel("time over two steps (s)")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The ZMP must be **under the stance foot** while the other foot swings — and
**under the other foot** for the next step. It cannot jump from one foot to the
other: it is a force-weighted average of contact points, and it can only be
between the feet while **both** feet are touching. The grey bands are when
the weight transfers.

Remove them and the ZMP must switch feet in an instant; at the very same
instant the new foot has just landed and the old one is already lifting. The
LIPM step then starts with an error — and errors grow ×7 per step (two slides
ago). Measured: with `double_support = 0` the robot falls at **2.0 s**.

---

## Assembling the controller {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 2.6)); ax.axis("off"); ax.set_xlim(0, 10); ax.set_ylim(0, 2.6)
blocks = [(0.1, "time $t$", "0.6"), (1.7, "which step?\nhow far in?", "#7f8c8d"),
          (3.5, "CoM target\n(LIPM, BVP)", "#3b7dd8"), (5.3, "foot targets\n(plan + swing)", "#e8743b"),
          (7.1, "IK: 12 leg\nangles", "#8e44ad"), (8.7, "29 servos\n→ physics", "#2a9d5c")]
for x, label, c in blocks:
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((x, 0.8), 1.25, 1.0, color=c, alpha=0.85))
    ax.text(x + 0.62, 1.3, label, ha="center", va="center", color="w", fontsize=9, weight="bold")
for x0_, x1_ in ((1.35, 1.7), (2.95, 3.5), (4.75, 5.3), (6.55, 7.1), (8.35, 8.7)):
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x1_, 1.3), xytext=(x0_, 1.3), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=1.5))
ax.text(5.0, 0.3, "open loop: nothing comes back from the physics", ha="center", fontsize=9, color="#c0392b")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Every control cycle, at 500 Hz:

1. **Which step** are we in, and how far through it ($s$)?
2. **Where should the body be?** The step's LIPM solution at time $sT$ gives the CoM (= pelvis) target.
3. **Where should each foot be?** The stance foot stays planted; the swing foot follows $x_{\text{foot}}(\sigma), z_{\text{foot}}(\sigma)$.
4. **What joint angles?** Week 3's damped-least-squares IK, both legs.
5. **Send** those angles to the position servos (week 5 opens this box).

---

## One trap: the singularity {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
from soc4180 import kinematics as kin
site, dof, qi = kin.foot_site_id(model, "left"), kin.leg_dof_indices(model, "left"), kin.leg_qpos_indices(model, "left")
scratch = mujoco.MjData(model)
knees = np.linspace(0, 1.2, 41); smin = []
for k in knees:
    scratch.qpos[:] = model.key_qpos[0]
    scratch.qpos[qi[0]], scratch.qpos[qi[3]], scratch.qpos[qi[4]] = -k / 2, k, -k / 2     # a crouch, foot level
    mujoco.mj_forward(model, scratch)
    jp, jr = np.zeros((3, model.nv)), np.zeros((3, model.nv))
    mujoco.mj_jacSite(model, scratch, jp, jr, site)
    smin.append(np.linalg.svd(np.vstack([jp, jr])[:, dof], compute_uv=False).min())
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 2.7))
ax.semilogy(knees, smin, color="#8e44ad", lw=2)
ax.axvline(0.70, color="0.5", ls=":"); ax.text(0.71, 1.5e-4, "the walking crouch\n(knee 0.70 rad)", fontsize=8, color="0.4")
ax.set_xlabel("knee angle (rad); hip and ankle each −knee/2"); ax.set_ylabel(r"smallest singular value $\sigma_{\min}$")
ax.grid(alpha=0.3, which="both"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"sigma_min at a straight leg (knee 0): {smin[0]:.1e}     at the crouch: {np.interp(0.70, knees, smin):.3f}")
```

Week 3: IK solves $J\,\Delta q = \mathbf{e}$, and each direction is divided by
its singular value $\sigma_i$. With the leg **straight**, nothing can shorten
it — turning hip, knee or ankle a little only swings the foot along an arc,
never toward the hip — so the "shorten" direction has
$\sigma_{\min} \approx 10^{-6}$. Week 3 measured the cost: lowering the foot
5 cm from a straight leg asks for tens of thousands of radians, and damping
refuses to move at all. The G1's
`stand` keyframe has every leg joint at exactly zero. **So every gait starts
from a crouch**, where $\sigma_{\min}$ is 100,000 times larger. Humans do not
walk with locked knees either.

## What you just watched

A 29-degree-of-freedom humanoid walking, driven by:

- one second-order linear ODE, ${\color{#3b7dd8}{\ddot x}} = {\color{#c0392b}{\omega^2}}({\color{#3b7dd8}{x}} - {\color{#e8743b}{p}})$
- its closed-form solution, and one boundary value problem per step
- a periodic sideways sway with $y_0 = 0$
- a cycloid, and inverse kinematics

**No training. No data. No reward function.** Roughly two hundred lines.

Remember this when a walking policy takes 150 million simulation steps to learn
the same thing. Learning buys robustness, not the gait itself.

---

## Now measure it {.smaller}

Belief is not evidence. Where did the ZMP actually go? `controller.zmp(data)`
computes the CoP from MuJoCo's contact forces — the formula from the CoP slide:
$\sum f_i x_i / \sum f_i$ over every contact.

```{python}
controller = soc4180.WalkingController(model, soc4180.GaitParams(n_steps=12))
data = controller.initial_data()

log = []
while data.time < controller.total_time:
    data.ctrl[:] = controller.control(data.time)
    mujoco.mj_step(model, data)
    zx, zy = controller.zmp(data)
    log.append((data.time, data.qpos[0], data.qpos[1], data.qpos[2], zx, zy))

log = np.array(log)
walking = log[log[:, 0] > controller.params.settle_time]
grounded = walking[~np.isnan(walking[:, 4])]

print(f"travelled     {log[-1,1]:+.3f} m")
print(f"pelvis height [{log[:,3].min():.3f}, {log[:,3].max():.3f}] m — never fell")
print(f"ZMP y range   [{grounded[:,5].min():+.3f}, {grounded[:,5].max():+.3f}] m")
print(f"stance feet at +-{controller.params.stance_width:.3f} m")
```

---

## The model is wrong, usefully {.smaller}

```{python}
w_st = controller.params.stance_width
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9, 5), sharex=True)

ax[0].plot(grounded[:, 0], grounded[:, 5], lw=1.2, color="#e8743b", label="measured ZMP $y$")
ax[0].plot(walking[:, 0], walking[:, 2], lw=1.2, color="#3b7dd8", label="pelvis $y$")
for s_ in (+w_st, -w_st):
    ax[0].axhline(s_, ls="--", lw=0.8, color="0.4")
ax[0].set_ylabel("lateral (m)"); ax[0].legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8)
ax[0].set_title("dashed = stance foot centres")

ax[1].plot(walking[:, 0], walking[:, 1], lw=1.2, color="#3b7dd8")
ax[1].set_ylabel("forward $x$ (m)"); ax[1].set_xlabel("time (s)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Where the ZMP actually went {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.6, 3.2))
for k, (support, support_xy, swing_from, swing_to) in enumerate(controller.plan):
    for xy in (support_xy, swing_to):
        ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((xy[0] - 0.085, xy[1] - 0.03), 0.17, 0.06,
                                   color="#3b7dd8" if xy[1] > 0 else "#e8743b", alpha=0.25))
sc = ax.scatter(grounded[:, 4], grounded[:, 5], c=grounded[:, 0], s=4, cmap="viridis")
ax.plot(walking[:, 1], walking[:, 2], color="k", lw=1, label="pelvis")
plt.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, label="time (s)")
ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlabel("x forward (m)"); ax.set_ylabel("y left (m)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left"); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax.set_title("measured ZMP (dots) over the planned footprints (boxes)", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The dots should never leave a box. They do — by up to ten centimetres
sideways at every support exchange. That is not a measurement error; it is
the list on the next slide.

---

## Where the LIPM breaks {.smaller}

The measured ZMP swings **wider than the feet**. The theory says that cannot
happen with flat feet — and the theory is right; the assumptions are what failed:

| LIPM assumes | The G1 actually |
| --- | --- |
| A point mass | Has a swinging leg with real momentum |
| Constant CoM height | Bobs as the stance leg compresses |
| Massless legs | Carries ~30% of its mass below the hips |
| Instant support exchange | Rolls weight across a finite foot |
| Perfectly rigid position control | Uses servos of finite stiffness that sag |

It walks anyway. **A model does not have to be true to be useful — it has to be
wrong in ways that do not matter yet.** Weeks 11 and 12 are where they start to matter.

---

## The honest limitations {.smaller}

This controller is **open loop**. It never looks at the IMU, never measures where
the body actually is, and never corrects. In capture-point terms: it never
checks where ${\color{#8e44ad}{\xi}}$ is, so it cannot move a foot to catch it.

Consequences you can see in the data:

- it **drifts sideways** over many steps, with nothing to pull it back
- it cannot recover from a push, at all
- it walks on flat ground only — one unexpected step and it is over
- the gait is fixed at design time; asking for a different speed means
  re-deriving

Every one of these is a reason the field moved to feedback — capture-point
stepping, model-predictive control (week 11) and learned policies (weeks
8–13). **Not because the mathematics is wrong** — you just watched it work —
but because a plan made in advance is brittle outside the conditions it was
made for.

## Exercises {.smaller}

Break it deliberately, and record what fails and why.

1. **Derive it yourself.** Starting from $\ddot u = \omega^2 u$, $u(0) = x_0 - p$,
   $\dot u(0) = v_0$, find $A$ and $B$ and check the cosh/sinh form.
2. **The capture point.** Show that $\eta = x - \dot x/\omega$ obeys
   $\dot\eta = -\omega(\eta - p)$. What happens to $\eta$ if $p$ is held fixed?
3. **Remove double support.** Set `double_support=0.0`. How many steps before it
   falls? Which direction, and why that direction?
4. **Rush it.** Reduce `step_time` toward 0.35 s. Find the value where it fails.
   Compare it to $1/\omega$ — is the failure point near the model's own timescale?
5. **Moon.** Set gravity to $-1.62\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ **without** changing the
   controller. Predict the failure from $\omega = \sqrt{g/z_c}$ before running it.
6. **Instrument it.** Log $\xi = x + \dot x/\omega$ from the pelvis during the walk
   and plot it against the stance foot. When is it outside the foot?

## Next week

**05 — actuation and PD control.** Today we assumed the joints simply go
where they are told. They do not: they are position servos with finite gain,
and that is why the pelvis sagged below its commanded height all through this
lecture.

We tune those gains, measure tracking error against torque saturation, and then
build a gait with **no model at all** — a central pattern generator — to compare
against today's.
